summary: Writes down current practices for complaint feedback loops, where mailbox providers tell senders when users mark mail as spam. It is based on work from the Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group, not the IETF itself. The goal is to clarify how providers and receivers should use such feedback. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When people say "this is junk", the mail company can tell the sender, so the sender stops. This records the common good habits for how those reports are sent and used.

subtitle: How mailbox providers report spam complaints back to senders.

tldr.problem: Email senders have no direct way to know when their messages are marked as spam, making it hard to fix deliverability problems or reduce complaints.
tldr.mechanism: Complaint Feedback Loops (CFBLs) let mailbox providers automatically send reports to senders whenever a user marks an email as spam, enabling senders to take corrective action in real time.
tldr.outcome: Both mailbox providers and email senders benefit: providers get fewer false positives by giving senders a chance to improve, and senders can reduce complaint rates by acting on feedback.

today: RFC 6449 is an Informational RFC documenting industry best practices established by the Messaging Anti-Abuse Working Group. It is still current and widely referenced by mail providers and senders that implement complaint feedback loops.

sections.title: What a Complaint Feedback Loop Is
sections.content:
A Complaint Feedback Loop is a system where a mailbox provider (such as Gmail or Yahoo) automatically sends a report back to the sender of an email whenever an end user marks that email as spam. The report arrives by email, formatted in a standard way called the Abuse Reporting Format (ARF), and includes a copy of the original message. The goal is simple: let senders know they have a problem so they can fix it.

This feedback closes a gap that has existed in email since the beginning. Senders traditionally had no way to know whether their messages were being marked as spam, and mailbox providers had to guess whether complaints were legitimate or false positives. By linking the two, a feedback loop lets mailbox providers avoid wrongly blocking good senders, and it lets senders improve their practices.
sections.eli5: When someone clicks "this is spam", the mail company sends an automatic note to whoever sent the email. That way the sender can fix the problem.

sections.title: The Feedback Flow
sections.content:
The process involves three main roles. An end user clicks a "Report Spam" button in their mail client. The mailbox provider collects that complaint. The feedback provider (often the same company as the mailbox provider, but not always) processes the complaint and sends it to the feedback consumer (the person who sent the original email, or the organization they work for).

The mailbox provider verifies that the feedback consumer actually owns the IP address or domain from which the email was sent, using methods such as checking the Reverse DNS record or DKIM signature. This prevents spammers from signing up for feedback about domains or IP ranges they do not own.

One key principle: the mailbox provider does not review or judge the complaint before sending it. Every complaint is forwarded immediately, without any human analysis. This means some reports may turn out to be false positives (a user who misclicked, or an entire mailbox marked as spam by mistake), but the speed of the feedback is more important than perfection.
sections.eli5: A user says "this is junk". The mail company checks if the sender really owns their address. Then it sends the complaint to the sender, fast.

sections.title: For Mailbox Providers: Setting Up a Feedback Loop
sections.content:
A mailbox provider should collect complaints via a "Report Spam" button in its webmail or mail client interface. It should make this button easy to find and understand, and should educate users about what it does.

The mailbox provider must then vet applications from senders who want to receive feedback. This vetting should verify that the applicant really owns the IP addresses or domains they claim to manage. Tools such as ASN lookups, WHOIS records, Reverse DNS and DKIM signatures can automate much of this. The provider should also require a two-step enrollment process: the applicant fills out a form, then they must receive and acknowledge a confirmation email sent to an abuse@ or postmaster@ address at their domain.

The feedback provider should maintain a web site with FAQs, Terms of Service, and a way for enrolled parties to update their information. Contact email addresses for the Feedback Consumer should be validated over time, and IP address ownership should be re-validated periodically against current criteria to catch cases where an IP or domain has changed hands.
sections.eli5: The mail company asks senders to sign up and proves they own their IP address. It sends them a confirmation email, and checks that the list of IPs they listed is still correct.

sections.title: Privacy and Policy
sections.content:
A feedback loop crosses international borders and handles sensitive information: email addresses, IP addresses, and the contents of messages. A mailbox provider must comply with local privacy laws and regulations in all countries where it operates. For example, some European jurisdictions require specific approvals before certain data can be shared internationally.

The provider and the feedback consumer should agree in writing on a Terms of Use before any feedback is sent. The agreement should make clear that the data is provided to a specific, approved entity and should not be shared or used for purposes beyond the agreement. Feedback consumers should be reminded that feedback is a privilege that can be revoked at any time.

A feedback provider may redact information it considers private, such as the email address of the person who reported the spam or the IP address of their device. Some senders have large numbers of customers and mailing lists; the feedback provider should include enough information about which list the complaint concerns so the sender can identify which customer to contact.
sections.eli5: The mail company and sender have to promise to keep the information private. Email addresses and IP addresses of the people who complained may be hidden.

sections.title: For Senders: Handling Feedback
sections.content:
A sender should treat a feedback message as a serious signal. The person who reported the email explicitly marked it as spam, so the sender should assume they do not want to receive more messages from that sender. The recommended action is to remove the email address from future mailings or add it to a suppression list.

However, the decision is not always straightforward. If the sender runs a mailing list that people pay to receive, or if the email is a transactional message tied to a service (such as an airline ticket confirmation), the sender may need to use judgment. In extreme cases, a sender might ignore a complaint if it clearly seems like a mistake (for example, a customer reporting their own purchase confirmation as spam).

Large senders should track trends in complaints. A sudden spike from a particular IP address or customer might signal a compromised system. Comparing the complaint rate to the number of emails actually delivered can reveal whether a reputation system is filtering mail into the spam folder rather than the inbox. The complaint rate calculation is subtle; a sender that receives 10 complaints on a day when it sent only 500 emails in the inbox (but 10,000 total to bulk or spam folders) may have a much higher complaint rate than it appears.
sections.eli5: A sender should remove complaining addresses from their list. But if someone accidentally reported their own airline ticket, it is okay to ignore it and send the ticket anyway.

sections.title: The Abuse Reporting Format (ARF)
sections.content:
The Abuse Reporting Format, defined in RFC 5965, is the standard way feedback messages are sent. An ARF message is a MIME multipart/report email that contains three sections.

The first section is human-readable plain text, for the benefit of small senders who handle reports by hand. It typically says "This is a complaint feedback report" and provides URLs to contact the mailbox provider.

The second section contains machine-readable metadata: the ARF version, the type of report (abuse, fraud, etc.), and optional fields such as the original sender's address and the time the email was received. This section is mostly ignored in current practice, as most senders process the third section directly.

The third section is a copy of the original email being reported, as a message/rfc822 attachment. It may be modified: feedback providers often redact the recipient's email address or other fields to protect privacy.
sections.eli5: A feedback report is an email with three parts: a friendly note for humans, some data for computers, and a copy of the email that was reported as spam.
